grammarQuestions.question: He didn't ______ me the whole story yesterday.

title: Good vs. Well
description: Good describes a noun, well usually describes an action or health.

words.detail: Describes a noun; used after linking verbs like 'is' or 'looks'.
words.wrongExample: She sings very good.
words.correctExample: She is a good singer.

words.detail: Describes how an action is performed, or refers to health.
words.wrongExample: She is a well singer.
words.correctExample: She sings very well.

grammarQuestions.question: He did really ______ on his final exam.

title: Amount vs. Number
description: Amount is for uncountable nouns, number is for countable ones.

words.detail: Used with uncountable nouns, like quantities of something.
words.wrongExample: A large number of water was spilled.
words.correctExample: A large amount of water was spilled.

words.detail: Used with countable nouns, like items you can count.
words.wrongExample: A large amount of guests attended.
words.correctExample: A large number of guests attended.

grammarQuestions.question: A surprising ______ of students passed the exam this year.

title: Beside vs. Besides
description: One means next to, the other means in addition to.

words.detail: Next to or at the side of something.
words.wrongExample: Besides the river, there is a nice path.
words.correctExample: Beside the river, there is a nice path.

words.detail: In addition to, or apart from.
words.wrongExample: Beside pizza, what else would you like?
words.correctExample: Besides pizza, what else would you like?

grammarQuestions.question: ______ studying, she also works part-time on weekends.

title: Between vs. Among
description: Between is for two things, among is for more than two.

words.detail: Used when referring to exactly two people or things.
words.wrongExample: The prize was divided among the two winners.
words.correctExample: The prize was divided between the two winners.

words.detail: Used when referring to more than two people or things.
words.wrongExample: The prize was divided between the five winners.
words.correctExample: The prize was divided among the five winners.

grammarQuestions.question: The inheritance was split ______ the three siblings.

title: Can vs. May
description: Can refers to ability, may refers to permission (in formal usage).

words.detail: Refers to ability or possibility.
words.wrongExample: May you lift that heavy box?
words.correctExample: Can you lift that heavy box?

words.detail: Refers to permission, especially in formal contexts.
words.wrongExample: Can I leave early today, please?
words.correctExample: May I leave early today, please?

grammarQuestions.question: ______ I ask you a personal question?

title: Compose vs. Comprise
description: One means to make up a whole, the other means to contain parts.

words.detail: To make up or form the parts of a whole.
words.wrongExample: The committee comprises of ten members.
words.correctExample: Ten members compose the committee.

words.detail: To consist of or be made up of parts.
words.wrongExample: Ten members compose of the committee.
words.correctExample: The committee comprises ten members.

grammarQuestions.question: The orchestra ______ musicians from twenty different countries.

title: If vs. Whether
description: If introduces a condition, whether introduces a choice between alternatives.

words.detail: Introduces a condition.
words.wrongExample: I don't know whether it rains, we'll stay inside.
words.correctExample: If it rains, we'll stay inside.

words.detail: Introduces a choice between two or more alternatives.
words.wrongExample: I don't know if to go or stay.
words.correctExample: I don't know whether to go or stay.

grammarQuestions.question: She asked ______ or not I wanted to join the trip.

title: Maybe vs. May Be
description: One is an adverb meaning perhaps, the other is a verb phrase.

words.detail: Means 'perhaps' or 'possibly'.
words.wrongExample: He may be late, or he may be on time.
words.correctExample: Maybe he will arrive on time.

words.detail: Combines the modal 'may' with the verb 'be'.
words.wrongExample: Maybe the answer, but I'm not certain.
words.correctExample: That may be the answer, but I'm not certain.

grammarQuestions.question: There ______ a simpler solution to this problem.

title: A Lot vs. Alot
description: The correct spelling is always two separate words.

words.detail: Correct spelling meaning 'a large amount'; always two words.
words.wrongExample: I have alot of homework tonight.
words.correctExample: I have a lot of homework tonight.

words.detail: A common misspelling of 'a lot'; not a real word.
words.wrongExample: There is a lot of confusion around alot as a word.
words.correctExample: Remember that 'alot' is never correct; always write 'a lot'.

grammarQuestions.question: She has ______ of experience in graphic design.

title: Everyday vs. Every Day
description: One is an adjective, the other is an adverbial phrase meaning 'each day'.

words.detail: Describes something ordinary or used daily; comes before a noun.
words.wrongExample: I go for a walk every day routine.
words.correctExample: Wearing sneakers is part of my everyday routine.

words.detail: Means 'each day'; used to describe frequency.
words.wrongExample: I go for a walk everyday.
words.correctExample: I go for a walk every day.

grammarQuestions.question: He practices the piano ______ after school.

title: Anyone vs. Any One
description: Anyone means any person; any one emphasizes a single item from a group.

words.detail: Refers to any person, unspecified.
words.wrongExample: Any one can join the club if they'd like.
words.correctExample: Anyone can join the club if they'd like.

words.detail: Emphasizes a single person or item from a specific group.
words.wrongExample: Anyone of these books would make a great gift.
words.correctExample: Any one of these books would make a great gift.

grammarQuestions.question: ______ of the three options would work fine for me.

title: Awhile vs. A While
description: Awhile is an adverb, a while is a noun phrase usually following a preposition.

words.detail: Means 'for a short time'; not preceded by a preposition.
words.wrongExample: Let's rest for awhile before continuing.
words.correctExample: Let's rest awhile before continuing.

words.detail: Refers to a period of time; often follows 'for' or 'in'.
words.wrongExample: Let's rest for while before continuing.
words.correctExample: Let's rest for a while before continuing.

grammarQuestions.question: We waited ______ before the doctor finally called us in.

title: Already vs. All Ready
description: Already refers to time, all ready means completely prepared.

words.detail: By this time; refers to something that has happened.
words.wrongExample: We are all ready finished with dinner.
words.correctExample: We have already finished with dinner.

words.detail: Means completely prepared for something.
words.wrongExample: We are already for the trip tomorrow.
words.correctExample: We are all ready for the trip tomorrow.

grammarQuestions.question: The guests are ______ to begin the ceremony.

title: Altogether vs. All Together
description: Altogether means completely, all together means everyone/everything in one place.

words.detail: Means 'completely' or 'in total'.
words.wrongExample: The plan was all together different from what we expected.
words.correctExample: The plan was altogether different from what we expected.

words.detail: Means everyone or everything gathered in one place.
words.wrongExample: Let's stay altogether so we don't get separated.
words.correctExample: Let's stay all together so we don't get separated.

grammarQuestions.question: The cost of the trip came to $500 ______.

title: Nobody vs. No Body
description: Nobody means no person, no body refers literally to an absence of a physical body.

words.detail: Means 'no person' or 'not anyone'.
words.wrongExample: There was no body at the meeting.
words.correctExample: There was nobody at the meeting.

words.detail: Refers literally to the absence of a physical body.
words.wrongExample: The detectives found nobody at the crime scene, just evidence.
words.correctExample: The detectives found no body at the crime scene, just evidence.

grammarQuestions.question: ______ answered when I knocked on the door.

title: Sometime vs. Some Time
description: Sometime means at an unspecified point, some time refers to a duration.

words.detail: At an unspecified or unknown point in time.
words.wrongExample: I need some time to finish this, maybe next week.
words.correctExample: Let's meet up sometime next week.

words.detail: Refers to an amount or duration of time.
words.wrongExample: I need sometime to finish this project.
words.correctExample: I need some time to finish this project.

grammarQuestions.question: It will take ______ before the results are ready.

title: Toward vs. Towards
description: Both are correct; 'toward' is more common in American English, 'towards' in British English.

words.detail: American English preference; means 'in the direction of'.
words.wrongExample: She walked towards, the American editor preferred toward.
words.correctExample: She walked toward the front of the classroom.

words.detail: British English preference; means 'in the direction of'.
words.wrongExample: She walked toward the front, said the British author, who prefers towards.
words.correctExample: She walked towards the front of the classroom.

grammarQuestions.question: He slowly made his way ______ the exit.

title: Whom vs. Who
description: Who is a subject pronoun, whom is an object pronoun.

words.detail: Used when referring to the subject of a clause.
words.wrongExample: Whom is calling, please?
words.correctExample: Who is calling, please?

words.detail: Used when referring to the object of a verb or preposition.
words.wrongExample: Who did you give the letter to?
words.correctExample: To whom did you give the letter?

grammarQuestions.question: ______ should I address this letter to?

title: Each Other vs. One Another
description: Traditionally, each other is used for two, one another for more than two.

words.detail: Traditionally used when referring to exactly two people.
words.wrongExample: The five friends helped each other during the trip works fine informally.
words.correctExample: The two partners supported each other through the project.

words.detail: Traditionally used when referring to more than two people.
words.wrongExample: The two partners supported one another, though today either phrase is common.
words.correctExample: The five friends helped one another during the trip.

grammarQuestions.question: All the students in the group encouraged ______ before the exam.

title: Could Have vs. Could Of
description: The correct form uses 'have'; 'could of' is a common misspelling based on pronunciation.

words.detail: The grammatically correct form, often contracted to 'could've'.
words.wrongExample: I could of helped you if you had asked.
words.correctExample: I could have helped you if you had asked.

words.detail: A common error caused by the way 'could've' sounds when spoken.
words.wrongExample: Remember that 'could have' is correct, not 'could of'.
words.correctExample: Never write 'could of' in formal writing; use 'could have' instead.

grammarQuestions.question: She ______ finished the project earlier if she'd started sooner.

title: I vs. Me
description: I is a subject pronoun, me is an object pronoun.

words.detail: Used when the pronoun is the subject of the sentence.
words.wrongExample: Me and my brother went to the store.
words.correctExample: My brother and I went to the store.

words.detail: Used when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition.
words.wrongExample: Please give the book to my sister and I.
words.correctExample: Please give the book to my sister and me.

grammarQuestions.question: Just between you and ______, I think she's right.

title: Myself vs. Me
description: Myself is reflexive and refers back to the subject; it shouldn't replace 'me' or 'I'.

words.detail: Used when the subject and object of a sentence are the same person.
words.wrongExample: Please contact John or myself with questions.
words.correctExample: I taught myself how to play the guitar.

words.detail: The correct choice for an object pronoun; do not replace with 'myself' unnecessarily.
words.wrongExample: I hurt me while running yesterday.
words.correctExample: I hurt myself while running yesterday.

grammarQuestions.question: Please send the report to Sarah or ______.

title: Regardless vs. Irregardless
description: Regardless is the standard word; irregardless is considered nonstandard.

words.detail: Means 'without regard to' or 'despite'; the standard, correct form.
words.wrongExample: Irregardless of the weather, we're going hiking.
words.correctExample: Regardless of the weather, we're going hiking.

words.detail: A nonstandard variant often used in place of 'regardless'; best avoided in formal writing.
words.wrongExample: Please use regardless instead of irregardless in your essay.
words.correctExample: Avoid using 'irregardless'; standard English prefers 'regardless'.

grammarQuestions.question: She decided to go through with the plan ______ of the risks.

title: Bad vs. Badly
description: Bad is an adjective describing a noun, badly is an adverb describing a verb.

words.detail: Describes a noun or follows a linking verb like 'feel' or 'seem'.
words.wrongExample: I feel badly about what happened.
words.correctExample: I feel bad about what happened.

words.detail: Describes how an action is performed.
words.wrongExample: He played bad in the final match.
words.correctExample: He played badly in the final match.

grammarQuestions.question: The team performed really ______ during the second half.

title: Real vs. Really
description: Real is an adjective describing a noun, really is an adverb describing a verb or adjective.

words.detail: Describes a noun; means genuine or actual.
words.wrongExample: She was really happy about the real news.
words.correctExample: That was a real diamond, not a fake one.

words.detail: Modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb; means 'truly' or 'very'.
words.wrongExample: That was a real good movie, actually.
words.correctExample: That was a really good movie, actually.

grammarQuestions.question: I am ______ excited about the upcoming trip.

title: Bought vs. Brought
description: Bought is the past tense of 'buy', brought is the past tense of 'bring'.

words.detail: The past tense of 'to buy', meaning to purchase.
words.wrongExample: She brought a new car last week.
words.correctExample: She bought a new car last week.

words.detail: The past tense of 'to bring', meaning to carry something along.
words.wrongExample: He bought his dog to the picnic.
words.correctExample: He brought his dog to the picnic.

grammarQuestions.question: He ______ his notes to class so he could study during lunch.

title: Quiet vs. Quite
description: Quiet means silent, quite means to a certain extent or completely.

words.detail: Making little or no noise; calm and silent.
words.wrongExample: It was quite in the library.
words.correctExample: It was quiet in the library.

words.detail: Means 'to a certain degree' or 'completely'.
words.wrongExample: She was quiet tired after the long hike.
words.correctExample: She was quite tired after the long hike.

grammarQuestions.question: The house was ______ eerie at night.

title: Costume vs. Custom
description: Costume refers to clothing worn for a special occasion, custom refers to a tradition.

words.detail: An outfit worn for a special occasion, performance, or disguise.
words.wrongExample: It's a local custom to wear masks for the play.
words.correctExample: She wore a fantastic costume to the Halloween party.

words.detail: A traditional practice or way of doing something.
words.wrongExample: It is a common costume in that region to greet elders first.
words.correctExample: It is a common custom in that region to greet elders first.

grammarQuestions.question: Removing your shoes indoors is a ______ in many cultures.

title: Adapt vs. Adopt
description: Adapt means to adjust, adopt means to take on or take in.

words.detail: To adjust or become suited to new conditions.
words.wrongExample: They decided to adopt their plans to the new schedule.
words.correctExample: They decided to adapt their plans to the new schedule.

words.detail: To take on, accept, or legally take in as one's own.
words.wrongExample: The family plans to adapt a rescue dog next month.
words.correctExample: The family plans to adopt a rescue dog next month.

grammarQuestions.question: The company had to ______ quickly to the changing market.

title: Device vs. Devise
description: Device is a noun, devise is a verb meaning to plan or invent.

words.detail: A tool or piece of equipment made for a particular purpose.
words.wrongExample: We need to devise a new charger for this phone.
words.correctExample: We need to buy a new charging device for this phone.

words.detail: To plan or invent something through careful thought.
words.wrongExample: They need to device a new strategy for the game.
words.correctExample: They need to devise a new strategy for the game.

grammarQuestions.question: The engineers had to ______ a clever solution to the problem.

title: Prophecy vs. Prophesy
description: Prophecy is the noun, prophesy is the verb.

words.detail: A prediction, especially one made through divine inspiration.
words.wrongExample: The wizard began to prophecy about the future.
words.correctExample: The ancient prophecy foretold a great disaster.

words.detail: To predict or foretell something, often in a spiritual sense.
words.wrongExample: The ancient prophesy foretold a great disaster.
words.correctExample: The wizard began to prophesy about the future.

grammarQuestions.question: The old seer would often ______ about coming storms.

title: Breath vs. Breathe
description: Breath is a noun, breathe is the verb.

words.detail: The air taken into or let out of the lungs.
words.wrongExample: Take a deep breathe before you dive.
words.correctExample: Take a deep breath before you dive.

words.detail: To take air into and expel it from the lungs.
words.wrongExample: It's hard to breath in this thin mountain air.
words.correctExample: It's hard to breathe in this thin mountain air.

grammarQuestions.question: Remember to ______ slowly and stay calm during the exercise.

title: Cloth vs. Clothe
description: Cloth is a noun referring to fabric, clothe is a verb meaning to dress someone.

words.detail: A piece of woven or knitted fabric.
words.wrongExample: She used a soft clothe to wipe the table.
words.correctExample: She used a soft cloth to wipe the table.

words.detail: To dress or provide clothing for someone.
words.wrongExample: It's expensive to cloth a growing family.
words.correctExample: It's expensive to clothe a growing family.

grammarQuestions.question: Charities work hard to feed and ______ those in need.

title: Choose vs. Chose
description: Choose is the present tense, chose is the past tense.

words.detail: To select from a range of options, in the present.
words.wrongExample: Yesterday, she choose the blue dress.
words.correctExample: Today, she will choose the blue dress.

words.detail: The past tense of 'to choose'.
words.wrongExample: Tomorrow, she chose the blue dress.
words.correctExample: Yesterday, she chose the blue dress.

grammarQuestions.question: Last night, he ______ the chicken instead of the fish.

title: Except vs. Expect
description: Except means excluding, expect means to anticipate something.

words.detail: Meaning 'excluding' or 'apart from'.
words.wrongExample: I expect pizza, everyone likes salad.
words.correctExample: Except for pizza, everyone likes salad.

words.detail: To anticipate or believe something will happen.
words.wrongExample: I except you to arrive by noon.
words.correctExample: I expect you to arrive by noon.

grammarQuestions.question: We ______ the package to arrive sometime next week.

title: Moral vs. Morale
description: Moral relates to right and wrong, morale refers to confidence or spirit.

words.detail: Relating to principles of right and wrong, or a lesson.
words.wrongExample: Team morale of the story is to be honest.
words.correctExample: The moral of the story is to be honest.

words.detail: The confidence, enthusiasm, and discipline of a person or group.
words.wrongExample: The moral of the team improved after the win.
words.correctExample: The morale of the team improved after the win.

grammarQuestions.question: The coach gave a speech to boost team ______.

title: Career vs. Careen
description: Career refers to one's profession, careen means to swerve or lurch uncontrollably.

words.detail: A person's course of professional life or occupation.
words.wrongExample: The car began to career down the hill out of control.
words.correctExample: She built a successful career in medicine.

words.detail: To move swiftly and uncontrollably in a swerving motion.
words.wrongExample: She built a successful careen in medicine over the years.
words.correctExample: The car began to careen down the hill out of control.

grammarQuestions.question: The runaway cart began to ______ toward the busy street.

title: Conscious vs. Conscience
description: Conscious means awake or aware, conscience refers to one's moral sense.

words.detail: Awake and aware of one's surroundings.
words.wrongExample: Her conscience kept her awake during the surgery.
words.correctExample: The patient remained conscious during the surgery.

words.detail: An inner sense of right and wrong that guides behavior.
words.wrongExample: His conscious told him to return the wallet.
words.correctExample: His conscience told him to return the wallet.

grammarQuestions.question: A guilty ______ kept him from sleeping that night.

title: Eminent vs. Imminent
description: Eminent means famous or distinguished, imminent means about to happen.

words.detail: Famous and respected within a particular field.
words.wrongExample: The storm is imminent professor gave a lecture.
words.correctExample: The eminent professor gave a lecture on climate change.

words.detail: About to happen very soon.
words.wrongExample: The eminent storm forced everyone indoors.
words.correctExample: The imminent storm forced everyone indoors.

grammarQuestions.question: Experts warned that a market crash seemed ______.

title: Formally vs. Formerly
description: Formally means in a formal manner, formerly means at an earlier time.

words.detail: In a formal or official manner.
words.wrongExample: She was formerly introduced to the board of directors.
words.correctExample: She was formally introduced to the board of directors.

words.detail: At an earlier time; previously.
words.wrongExample: He was formally known as a professional athlete.
words.correctExample: He was formerly known as a professional athlete.

grammarQuestions.question: The building was ______ used as a train station.

title: Lightening vs. Lightning
description: Lightening means becoming lighter, lightning is the electrical flash during a storm.

words.detail: The act of making something lighter in weight or color.
words.wrongExample: A bolt of lightening struck the tree.
words.correctExample: Lightening the load made the hike easier.

words.detail: The flash of light produced by an electrical discharge during a storm.
words.wrongExample: Lightning the mood, she told a joke.
words.correctExample: A bolt of lightning struck the old oak tree.

grammarQuestions.question: We saw a flash of ______ just before the thunder rolled in.

title: Simple vs. Simplistic
description: Simple means easy or uncomplicated, simplistic means oversimplified in a negative way.

words.detail: Easy to understand; not complicated.
words.wrongExample: The solution was elegant but simplistic.
words.correctExample: The solution was elegant and simple.

words.detail: Treating a complex issue as if it were simpler than it really is.
words.wrongExample: His explanation was clear and simplistic in a good way.
words.correctExample: His explanation was overly simplistic and ignored key details.

grammarQuestions.question: Critics said the argument was ______ and ignored important nuances.
